```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Forecasts are often needed at several levels: for groups (here sex by
deprivation quintile), for their totals (each sex, each quintile) and for
the whole population. Forecasts made separately for each level do not add
up: the deaths forecast for England differ from the sum of the deaths
forecast for its parts. This vignette shows why, the two ways to coherent
forecasts, and how to keep a total that is trusted more than its parts.
The model is Lee-Carter, as a simple example; every model works the same
way.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
```

## The hierarchy

`mt_hierarchy()` describes how the strata add up: the quintiles to
England, the sexes to both sexes. `mt_aggregate_strata()` adds the totals
to the data, by summing deaths and exposures:

```{r}
h <- mt_hierarchy(sex = "both", quintile = list(total = "England"))
xa <- mt_aggregate_strata(x, h)
mt_strata(xa, h)[, .N, by = level]
```

Ten bottom series (sex by quintile) and eight totals: five quintiles for
both sexes, the two sexes for England, and England.

## Separate forecasts do not add up

One Lee-Carter model for each of the 18 strata:

```{r}
fc_base <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), xa), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
mt_plot_coherence(fc_base, h)
```

The figure shows, for every total and year, the ratio of the sum of the
parts to the forecast of the total. In the median the two agree within a
few per cent, but the paths do not: the model of England and the models of
its parts draw their futures independently, so a path of England has no
matching paths of its parts.

## Two ways to coherent forecasts

* **Bottom-up**: forecast only the bottom series and add them up. The
  totals are then sums by construction (`method = "bottom_up"`).
* **Reconciliation**: forecast every stratum, then adjust all forecasts,
  path by path, so that they add up. The methods differ in which strata
  absorb the adjustment: `"wls"` moves each stratum in proportion to the
  uncertainty of its forecast, `"mint"` also uses how the strata move
  together (Wickramasuriya et al. 2019), `"ols"` moves all strata by the
  same number of deaths, and `"structural"` moves the totals more than the
  bottom series.

`mt_reconcile()` applies a method to forecasts; `reconciled()` makes it
part of a model, so that backtests reconcile at each origin.

```{r}
fc <- list(separate = fc_base,
           "bottom-up" = mt_reconcile(fc_base, h, method = "bottom_up"),
           wls = mt_reconcile(fc_base, h, method = "wls", seed = 1),
           mint = mt_reconcile(fc_base, h, method = "mint", seed = 1))
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 4.5}
mt_plot_compare(fc, periods = 2035, strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5", "male.Q1", "male.Q5", "both.Q1",
                                               "both.Q5", "female.England", "male.England", "both.England"))
```

Life expectancy at birth in 2035 for some of the strata. The medians move
little; the intervals change more. Separate models draw their paths
independently, and the reconciliation does not reorder them
(`dependence = "none"`, the default). Sums of independent parts vary less
than the totals' own forecasts, so the totals get much narrower intervals
under every method. WLS and MinT give almost the same result: MinT
estimates how the strata move together from the base draws, and the draws
of separate models do not move together.

## Keeping a trusted total

Sometimes one stratum is trusted more than the others: an official
projection of the total population, or an all-cause forecast that the
causes of death must add up to. `fixed` keeps such strata unchanged in
every path, and the others absorb the whole adjustment. With `"wls"` the
most uncertain parts absorb it; with `"proportional"` all parts are
scaled in proportion to their own forecasts (top-down allocation,
Athanasopoulos et al. 2009), which keeps their composition and never sets
a part to zero:

```{r}
fixed <- list(separate = fc_base,
              "wls, England fixed" = mt_reconcile(fc_base, h, method = "wls", fixed = "total", seed = 1),
              "proportional, England fixed" = mt_reconcile(fc_base, h, method = "proportional", fixed = "total",
                                                           seed = 1))
mt_compare_forecasts(fixed, periods = 2035, strata = c("both.England", "female.England", "female.Q1", "male.Q5"),
                     digits = 2)
```

England keeps the life expectancy of its own model; its parts move
towards it. The intervals of the bottom series widen (women in Q1, men in
Q5), because they now carry the uncertainty of England's own forecast.
With WLS, the projection would make some bottom forecasts negative. The
non-negative reconciliation of Wickramasuriya, Turlach and Hyndman (2020)
then minimises the same weighted distance with all bottom forecasts at
zero or above; in 10% of the draws some bottom forecasts end at zero (the
warning above).

## Does coherence cost accuracy?

A backtest from the origins 2010-2014, five years ahead, with the
reconciliation inside each fit:

```{r}
bt <- mt_compare(list(separate = lee_carter(),
                      "bottom-up" = reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "bottom_up"),
                      wls = reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "wls"),
                      mint = reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "mint")),
                 xa, origins = 2010:2014, h = 5, n_draws = 200)
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "cov95"), hierarchy = h)
```

`hierarchy = h` scores the bottom series (sex by quintile), the
aggregates (quintiles for both sexes, England by sex) and the total
(England) separately.

The bottom series are forecast about as well with every method (CRPS
0.067-0.068), and their coverage falls a little with WLS and MinT (0.77
against 0.79). The totals lose accuracy and much coverage: the 95%
intervals of England contain 0.37-0.42 of the observed rates after
reconciliation, against 0.67 with its own model. The model of England
captures the common movements of the quintiles in its trend; sums of
parts with independent draws do not reproduce them, so their intervals
are too narrow. Joint models such as `li_lee()` tie the parts together in
the model itself. `dependence = "empirical"` reorders the paths of
separately fitted parts so that they move together as they did in the
training years. This reordering is specific to this package, related to
the Schaake shuffle (Clark et al. 2004); it is used only when chosen, and
a backtest should check its effect. The vignette "Dependence between
groups" compares joint models and ensemble copula coupling for totals and
gaps.

## Reconciliation learnt from past forecasts

The methods above fix in advance how forecasts are adjusted. Score-optimal
reconciliation (Panagiotelis et al. 2023) learns the adjustment from the
base model's own forecasts of past years instead: `reconciled()` with
`method = "energy_score"` refits the base model at `n_origins` inner
origins within the last `years` of the training data, and estimates for
each age a correction `d` and a projection `G` of the base draws that
minimise the energy score of these forecasts, a multivariate CRPS of all
strata together. The reconciled draws `S (d + G y)` add up by
construction.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
so <- reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "energy_score", years = 6, n_origins = 5, horizon = 3)
fit <- mt_fit(so, xa)
fit$reconcile$scoreopt$table   # in-sample energy score with OLS and after the optimisation
```

Each fit takes about 20 seconds on these data, so the code is not run
here. In an example backtest from 2011 to 2014, the method was less
accurate than WLS at every level: CRPS 21% higher for the bottom series,
23% for the aggregates and 26% for England. The
training forecasts were too high in 2006-2011 and the correction learnt
from them pushed the forecasts down, while mortality improvement stalled
after 2011. With few, overlapping training forecasts and one parameter per
pair of strata at each age, the method follows the errors of the training
years; it suits long and stable histories, and a backtest should confirm
it.

## Choosing a method

* **Bottom-up** with a joint model of the parts keeps the detailed
  forecasts and needs no forecasts of the totals.
* **WLS** for reconciling separate forecasts. With separate models, whose
  draws are independent, **MinT** gives about the same result, and the
  intervals of the totals are too narrow; check their coverage in a
  backtest.
* **fixed** with **proportional** for a trusted total, for example causes
  of death that must add up to an all-cause forecast.
* **energy_score** only with long training histories, after a backtest
  against WLS.
* Check the choice at every level of the hierarchy in a backtest, as
  above. The applied vignettes use these methods for causes of death and
  German Laender.

Athanasopoulos G, Ahmed RA, Hyndman RJ (2009). Hierarchical forecasts for
Australian domestic tourism. *International Journal of Forecasting* 25:
146-166.

Clark M, Gangopadhyay S, Hay L, Rajagopalan B, Wilby R (2004). The Schaake
shuffle: a method for reconstructing space-time variability in forecasted
precipitation and temperature fields. *Journal of Hydrometeorology* 5(1):
243-262.

Panagiotelis A, Gamakumara P, Athanasopoulos G, Hyndman RJ (2023).
Probabilistic forecast reconciliation: properties, evaluation and score
optimisation. *European Journal of Operational Research* 306(2): 693-706.

Wickramasuriya SL, Athanasopoulos G, Hyndman RJ (2019). Optimal forecast
reconciliation for hierarchical and grouped time series through trace
minimization. *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 114(526):
804-819.

Wickramasuriya SL, Turlach BA, Hyndman RJ (2020). Optimal non-negative
forecast reconciliation. *Statistics and Computing* 30: 1167-1182.
